public_summary: Jungle Chess played with the solar system. Every piece is a planet, and a planet's size on the board is the fifth root of its real measured diameter, so rank is something you can see rather than learn: Mercury is the smallest world in play and Jupiter the largest, and the traditional rules are followed exactly as written. Matter faces antimatter. One army's worlds lean their poles one way and the other army's lean the other, by each planet's own true axial tilt, and the bases say it again in white against black. Four of the eight wear a real map -- Earth its coastlines, Mars its dark continents, Mercury its smooth plains with the Caloris basin in them, and Venus the radar surface no eye has seen. Three more wear their weather. One wears nothing at all, and that is what this edition changes. The change is unusual enough to say at the top: nothing was broken. The owner did not like the look of the two pale discs on Uranus, so they are gone. It wore an upright white band around its equator, then a broad soft polar hood at each pole; both were argued at length and measured twice, and the owner has looked at the finished hoods and taken them out. Nothing replaced them. Its globe is now one undivided cyan sphere -- no hood, no cap, no band, no spot -- and it is the only bare world in the box. A bare world is the right answer on this one: the reference is an almost featureless sphere, and what carries the piece is the ring, the size and the cyan. The ring turns white too, the same spool Saturn's ring prints from, so both ringed worlds now print their ring in white and the set's rule that rings are white holds without a footnote for the first time. Neither change moves a surface: both Uranus pieces come out byte-for-byte identical to the last edition's, which is the check this run turns on. The argument the owner overruled is kept word for word in the source. Nothing else in the set changed.
